# Breather and particle reflection amplitudes {#sec-particle-reflection}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Derive the reflection amplitude of the lowest breather from a soliton reflection matrix by the boundary bootstrap, and recognize Ghoshal's sine-Gordon result as its rank-one case.
- State precisely what has to be assumed to continue breather amplitudes in the coupling to the reflection amplitudes of the real-coupling particles, and what supports it.
- Know the $a_n^{(1)}$ particle reflection amplitudes for the uniform, Neumann and solitonic boundaries, and check them against unitarity, crossing-unitarity, the bootstrap, the classical limit and one-loop perturbation theory.
- Understand why weak–strong duality is not a symmetry of a half-line theory, but maps the uniform boundary to the Neumann boundary.
- Read a spectrum of boundary bound states off the poles of reflection amplitudes, and explain the remaining poles by boundary Coleman–Thun diagrams, for $a_2^{(1)}$.
- Know the open problems of affine Toda theory on the half-line.
:::

On the full line, the S-matrices of the real-coupling particles were found by bootstrap from their poles (@sec-simply-laced), and only later recovered from the soliton S-matrices of the imaginary-coupling theory, by building the lowest breather and continuing it in the coupling (@sec-breather-test). On the half-line the order is reversed. A real-coupling reflection amplitude has poles from boundary bound states, and nothing in the Lagrangian tells us in advance what those states are, so the axioms of @sec-boundary-scattering leave too much freedom. Early conjectures that fixed the freedom by demanding weak–strong self-duality turned out to be wrong. What worked was the route through the solitons: take the soliton reflection matrix of @sec-soliton-reflection, bootstrap it to the lowest breather, and continue in $\beta$. This is the method of Gandenberger for $a_2^{(1)}$ [@gandenberger1999a] and of Delius and Gandenberger for $a_n^{(1)}$ [@delius_gandenberger1999].

This chapter follows that route. It also closes Part VII, so its last section collects the open problems of the whole part. The amplitudes here are diagonal and are written in the blocks $(x)$ and $\{x\}$ of (-@eq-blocks), with $h=n+1$ and $B$ of (-@eq-b-of-beta). All their properties stated below, unless marked otherwise, are checked exactly (to 20 digits at random complex rapidities and couplings) in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`. We write DG for [@delius_gandenberger1999] when citing its equation numbers.

## Breather reflection amplitudes {#sec-breather-reflection}

Work at imaginary coupling, with $\omega=4\pi/\beta^2-1$ as in Part VI, and use Delius and Gandenberger's variables: $\mu=-\frac{iT\theta}\pi$ with $T=\frac{h\omega}2$, and the blocks

$$
(a)_I=\frac{\sin\frac{\pi(\mu+a)}{h\omega}}{\sin\frac{\pi(\mu-a)}{h\omega}} .
$$

Since $\frac{\pi\mu}{h\omega}=-\frac{i\theta}2$, $(a)_I$ is the block $(x)$ of (-@eq-blocks) with $x=2a/\omega$. The fundamental soliton multiplet $V$ (species 1) and its conjugate $\bar V$ (species $n$) bind at $\mu=\frac{h\omega}2-1$ into the lowest breather $B_1$, a singlet of $U_q(\hat g)$, whose S-matrices are those of the lightest real-coupling particle continued in the coupling (@sec-breather-test).

**The bootstrap.** Let $B_1$ come in with rapidity $\mu$. Its constituents, a soliton and an antisoliton with rapidities $\mu\pm(\frac{h\omega}4-\frac12)$, reflect in turn, scattering once in between at rapidity $2\mu$; projecting the result onto $B_1$ gives its reflection amplitude (@eq-boundary-bootstrap-bulk, in matrix form). For the diagonal reflection matrix $K=A(\theta)\mathbf 1:v_i\mapsto\bar v_i$ of @sec-an-diagonal-k, each constituent is reflected into its antiparticle, and the reflected pair is again a singlet. That is why the breather is reflected diagonally, as a real-coupling particle must be. Delius and Gandenberger carried out the projection, with the minimal scalar factor $A$ of (-@eq-an-diagonal-scalar), and found [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (3.11)]

$$
K_{B_1}(\mu)=\Big(-\frac n2\omega\Big)_I\Big(\frac12-\frac h2\omega\Big)_I\Big(-\frac\omega2-\frac12\Big)_I .
$$ {#eq-breather-k-imaginary}

::: {#prp-breather-amplitude}
## The lowest-breather reflection amplitude
**[Established]** For the soliton reflection matrix $K=A\,\mathbf 1$ of (-@eq-an-diagonal-k) with the minimal scalar factor (-@eq-an-diagonal-scalar), the lowest breather of $a_n^{(1)}$ is reflected with the amplitude (-@eq-breather-k-imaginary) [@gandenberger1999a; @delius_gandenberger1999]. For $n=1$, (-@eq-breather-k-imaginary) equals Ghoshal's lowest-breather factor (-@eq-bsg-b1-reflection) at $\eta=\frac\pi2$, $\vartheta=0$, the point where the coideal parameters $\hat\epsilon_0=\hat\epsilon_1$ vanish (@sec-bsg-parameters). The derivation is checked at the level of matrices for $n=1$ (@prp-bsg-breather-k) and for $n=2,3$.
:::

For $n=1$ the identity with Ghoshal's formula is checked in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`, and the matrix-level projection in `textbook_code/boundary_sine_gordon.py`. For $n\ge2$ the projection is simple. After the first reflection the singlet becomes $\sum_ic_i\,v_i\otimes v_i$, a sum of identical-soliton states, on which $\check R$ acts by its identical-soliton eigenvalue, normalized to 1. So

$$
K_{B_1}(\mu)=A\Big(\mu-\frac{h\omega}4+\frac12\Big)\,F_{11}(2\mu)\,A\Big(\mu+\frac{h\omega}4-\frac12\Big),
$$

and with (-@eq-an-diagonal-scalar) this equals (-@eq-breather-k-imaginary). We checked the matrix projection for $n=2,3$ with the book's $\check R$, and the scalar identity for $n=1,2,3$ (`textbook_code/reflection_matrices.py`). The prefactor of (-@eq-an-diagonal-scalar) matters: with $-(\frac h4\omega)_I$ in place of $(-\frac h4\omega)_I$, the product acquires the factor $f(\mu_a)f(\mu_b)$ with $f=-(1-i\sinh\theta)/(1+i\sinh\theta)$, and for $n=1$ it would contradict Ghoshal. Gandenberger gives the details for $a_2^{(1)}$ [@gandenberger1999a, appendix].

**Other soliton reflection matrices.** The same bootstrap applied to the two non-diagonal matrices (-@eq-an-k-matrix) ($s=\pm1$) gives two further breather amplitudes. For $a_2^{(1)}$ Gandenberger computed all three [@gandenberger1999a, eqs. (5.16)–(5.18)]. For both signs the scalar factor and the breather amplitude are now known for $n\le4$ (@prp-an-nondiagonal-scalar). For $s=+1$ they give the Neumann amplitude, and for $s=-1$ the "third matrix" amplitudes (@sec-neumann-duality).

**Soliton-preserving matrices.** For the matrices of @sec-preserving-conjugating the lowest breather comes back as its conjugate. Reflect the singlet in $V(\theta_a)\otimes\bar V(\theta_b)$ with $\tilde bK_{\bar V}$ and $aK_V$ of @prp-sp-scalar, with the bulk factor $F(2\mu)$ in between. The result is the singlet in $\bar V(-\theta_b)\otimes V(-\theta_a)$ times
$$
K_{1\to n}(\mu)=e^{-2\pi il/h}K_0(\mu)E_\eta(\theta),\qquad
K_0=\Big(\frac T2\Big)_I\Big(\frac T2-\frac12\Big)_I(\delta)_I\Big(\frac12-\delta\Big)_I\Big(\frac12+\delta\Big)_I\Big(T-\frac12-\delta\Big)_I,\quad\delta=\frac{T-\omega}2,
$$
$$
E_\eta(\theta)=\frac{\sinh\theta-i\sin\frac{\pi A}T}{\sinh\theta+i\sin\frac{\pi\bar A}T},\qquad A=\varepsilon+\frac{T-1}2,\quad\bar A=A+\omega l-T,
$$ {#eq-sp-breather}
and by $\sigma(\mu_a)\sigma(T-\mu_b)$ for a CDD factor $\sigma$. The reverse transition $\bar B_1\to B_1$ has $A\leftrightarrow\bar A$ and the phase $e^{2\pi il/h}$.

- **The phase.** It depends on the relative normalization of the two singlets. Here each has coefficient 1 on the highest weight of its left factor times the lowest weight of its right factor. For $n=1$, where the two singlets coincide, this is not a choice.
- **$l=0$ and $l=h$.** Then $E_\eta=1$, since $\eta$ enters $K_V$ only through a scalar.
- **$n=1$.** For $l=1$ and $\sigma=(-\frac T2)_I^2$, (-@eq-sp-breather) is Ghoshal's Dirichlet $K_{B_1}$, (-@eq-bsg-b1-reflection) with $\vartheta\to\infty$.

Continued by $\omega\to-2/B$,
$$
K_0\to\frac{(\frac h2)(\frac h2+\frac B2)(\frac h2-1)(\frac h2-1-\frac B2)(\frac h2+1+\frac B2)}{(\frac h2-1+\frac B2)} .
$$
The particle amplitudes $L_a=K_{a\to h-a}$ are given by the bulk boundary bootstrap, $L_c(\theta)=L_a(\theta+iu_a)\,S_{a,h-b}(2\theta+iu_a-iu_b)\,L_b(\theta-iu_b)$. They satisfy unitarity, $L_a(\theta)L_{h-a}(-\theta)=1$, and crossing-unitarity, $L_a(\frac{i\pi}2-\theta)=S_{aa}(2\theta)L_a(\frac{i\pi}2+\theta)$. For reflection into the conjugate the pair in the boundary state is $aa$, so $S_{aa}$ replaces the $S_{a\bar a}$ of (-@eq-boundary-crossing-diagonal). The bootstrap closes at every fusing, and $L_n$ is the soliton-side $K_{n\to1}$. This holds for the minimal factor and for the CDD factors allowed by the soliton bootstrap that we tested, while $(-\frac T2)_I^2$ breaks it for even $n$. As $B\to0$, $L_1\to e^{-2\pi il/h}g_{h/2}\,g_{h/2-1}\,E_\eta$ for all these factors, with $g_x=(\sinh\theta+i\sin\frac{\pi x}h)/(\sinh\theta-i\sin\frac{\pi x}h)$. This depends on $\theta$ when $h\ge3$ (`textbook_code/sp_scalar.py`).

## From breathers to particles {#sec-continuation-assumptions}

On the full line, the S-matrix of the lightest particles of the real-coupling theory is the S-matrix of the lowest breather continued in the coupling, $\beta^2\to-\beta^2$. In the sine-Gordon case this is the statement that the sinh-Gordon particle is the continued $B_1$ (@sec-sg-breather-particle). For $a_n^{(1)}$ it was found by Gandenberger and is the breather test of @sec-breather-test. Under $\beta^2\to-\beta^2$, $\omega=4\pi/\beta^2-1$ becomes $-4\pi/\beta^2-1=-2/B$, with $B$ of (-@eq-b-of-beta) (@exr-sg-continuation). The block $(a)_I=(2a/\omega)$ therefore becomes $(-aB)$, and (-@eq-breather-k-imaginary) becomes

$$
K_1(\theta)=(-n)\Big(h-\frac B2\Big)\Big(-1+\frac B2\Big)=\frac{(h-\frac B2)}{(h-1)\,(1-\frac B2)} ,
$$ {#eq-breather-continuation}

which is DG (3.12). Every factor here is a block $(x)$ of (-@eq-blocks), not a number: $(h-\frac B2)$ is the block at $x=h-\frac B2$. The second form uses $(-x)=(x)^{-1}$, so that $(-n)=(h-1)^{-1}$ and $(-1+\frac B2)=(1-\frac B2)^{-1}$. On the half-line, three more things have to continue: the boundary condition, the vacuum, and the identification of the soliton reflection matrix with that boundary condition. Delius and Gandenberger list the assumptions behind their amplitudes [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 7]. In our words:

1. **Minimality.** The scalar factor of the soliton reflection matrix is the minimal solution (-@eq-an-diagonal-scalar) of unitarity and crossing-unitarity, with no CDD factor (-@eq-an-cdd). After continuation, a soliton CDD factor $\sigma_c$ gives the particle factor $k_c=(\frac h2+c+\frac B2)(\frac h2-c-\frac B2)(-\frac h2+c-\frac B2)(-\frac h2-c+\frac B2)$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (3.25)], which is unitary, satisfies the crossing condition of a boundary CDD factor (@sec-boundary-unitarity-crossing) and tends to 1 as $B\to0$. It is excluded only because its extra poles appear to have no explanation, and this has not been analysed in detail.
2. **Vacua.** The vacuum of the real-coupling theory is the regular static solution of lowest energy: $\vec\phi=0$ for the uniform and Neumann boundaries, and the continued stationary soliton of @prp-solitonic-vacua for the solitonic ones. Lowest energy is believed, not proved (@sec-real-coupling-vacua).
3. **Continuation.** The reflection amplitudes of the particles about that vacuum are the breather amplitudes continued by $\omega\to-2/B$, with the boundary parameters $C_j$ held fixed.

The third assumption is the boundary analogue of the breather test, and we state it as a conjecture.

::: {#cnj-reflection-continuation}
## Continuation of reflection amplitudes
**[Conjecture]** Let a soliton-conjugating boundary of imaginary-coupling $a_n^{(1)}$ theory with parameters $C_j$ have soliton reflection matrix $K$, and let the real-coupling theory with the same $C_j$ have a vacuum obtained by continuing an imaginary-coupling static solution. Then the reflection amplitude of particle $a$ about that vacuum is the reflection amplitude of the breather $B_1^{(a)}$, computed by the boundary bootstrap from $K$ (and from the static soliton, @sec-solitonic-boundaries), continued by $\omega\to-2/B$.
:::

The evidence, in decreasing order of strength:

- **Sine-Gordon and sinh-Gordon.** For $n=1$ the conjecture gives the sinh-Gordon reflection factor (-@eq-shg-reflection) from Ghoshal's breather factor. That factor agrees with one-loop perturbation theory [@chenaghlou_corrigan2000] and with the semiclassical quantization of the boundary breathers (@sec-shg-boundary-breathers), which gives the relation between its parameter $E$ and the Lagrangian; the constant $N_0$ in that relation is fitted (@cnj-shg-e).
- **Classical limits.** The continued amplitudes of the uniform and Neumann boundaries tend, as $B\to0$, to the linearized reflection factors (-@eq-linear-reflection) of the vacuum $\vec\phi=0$ (@sec-uniform-boundary, @sec-neumann-duality). For the solitonic boundaries the limit (DG (5.7)) is Bowcock's linearized factor about the continued vacuum [@bowcock1998, (4.14), (4.21), (4.22)] (@prp-solitonic-linear).
- **One loop.** The Neumann amplitudes agree at $O(\beta^2)$ with Kim's one-loop calculation for $a_3^{(1)}$ [@kim1995], and for $a_2^{(1)}$ Gandenberger reports agreement with Kim's one-loop formulas [@gandenberger1999a, sec. 6] (@sec-neumann-duality). The uniform amplitude for $a_2^{(1)}$ agrees at $O(\beta^2)$ with Perkins and Bowcock [@perkins_bowcock1999, (5.5)] after a finite boundary counterterm whose coefficient they fix by the bootstrap. (Checked in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`; their (5.3) and (5.5) each lack a factor $i$.)
- **Thermodynamic Bethe ansatz.** Ahn, Kim and Rim report non-perturbative checks of the uniform and Neumann amplitudes of $a_n^{(1)}$, and of the boundary vacuum energies, by the boundary TBA [@akr2002] (cited, not checked here).
- **Semiclassics of the solitons.** The scalar factor $A$ reproduces the classical time delay of the $C\equiv+1$ boundary (@prp-semiclassical-uniform). This supports assumption 1 only up to CDD factors, which the time delay does not see.
- **Consistency.** The resulting amplitudes satisfy all the axioms, and for $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_4^{(1)}$ every physical-strip pole is explained by a boundary bound state or a boundary Coleman–Thun diagram (@sec-boundary-spectrum-a2). Delius and Gandenberger call this the a posteriori justification of the continuation.

The conjecture is stated for fixed $C_j$, which is unproblematic for $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$, where the $C_j$ are discrete. For $n=1$ the parameters are continuous and are renormalized, and fixed $C_j$ is not meaningful beyond the classical limit (@sec-uniform-boundary).

## The uniform boundary condition {#sec-uniform-boundary}

For the uniform boundary $C_j\equiv+1$ the vacuum is $\vec\phi=0$ (@exr-uniform-vacuum), and its soliton reflection matrix is the diagonal $K=A\,\mathbf 1$ (@cnj-neumann-coideal). The amplitude of the lightest particle is (-@eq-breather-continuation). Those of the heavier particles follow from the bulk boundary bootstrap (-@eq-boundary-bootstrap-bulk). In $a_n^{(1)}$, particles $a$ and $b$ with $a+b<h$ fuse to $a+b$ at $\theta=i\pi(a+b)/h$, and the constituents of $a+b$ at rapidity $\theta$ have rapidities $\theta+\frac{i\pi b}h$ and $\theta-\frac{i\pi a}h$, so

$$
K_{a+b}(\theta)=K_a\Big(\theta+\frac{i\pi b}h\Big)\,S_{ab}\Big(2\theta+\frac{i\pi(b-a)}h\Big)\,K_b\Big(\theta-\frac{i\pi a}h\Big) ,
$$

DG (3.13). Iterating from $K_1$ and simplifying with (-@eq-an-smatrix) gives DG (3.16). In the book's blocks,

$$
K_a(\theta)=\prod_{c=1}^a\frac{(c-1)\,\big(h+1-c-\frac B2\big)}{(h-c)\,\big(c-\frac B2\big)} .
$$ {#eq-uniform-amplitude}

::: {#prp-uniform-amplitude}
## Properties of the uniform amplitude
**[Numerical]** For $n=1,\dots,7$ and all $a$, the amplitudes (-@eq-uniform-amplitude):

(i) follow from (-@eq-breather-continuation) by iterating the bootstrap (DG (3.15)), and satisfy the bulk boundary bootstrap (-@eq-boundary-bootstrap-bulk) at every fusing of $a_n^{(1)}$, including those with $a+b>h$;
(ii) satisfy boundary unitarity (-@eq-boundary-unitarity), and crossing-unitarity both in the form (-@eq-boundary-crossing-diagonal) with $S_{a\bar a}$ from (-@eq-an-smatrix) and in DG's form $K_a(\theta)K_{\bar a}(\theta+i\pi)=S_{aa}(2\theta)$;
(iii) are charge-conjugation invariant, $K_a=K_{h-a}$;
(iv) tend, as $B\to0$, to $-1/\big((a)(h-a)\big)$, the linearized reflection factor (-@eq-linear-reflection) at $C=+1$;
(v) equal the conjecture of Corrigan, Dorey, Rietdijk and Sasaki for this boundary, their (5.16) with $\langle x\rangle$ replaced by $\widetilde{\langle x\rangle}$ [@cdrs1994].
:::

Checked in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`. That (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) is the reflection amplitude of $C\equiv+1$ is @cnj-reflection-continuation applied to @prp-breather-amplitude. Item (iv) is the classical counterpart of the assignment of the diagonal soliton reflection matrix to $C\equiv+1$ rather than to Neumann (@sec-epsilon-constraint). The linearized calculation of @sec-classical-reflection-factors knows nothing about solitons or coideals, yet it picks out the same boundary. Item (v) is a nice piece of history. Corrigan et al. wrote (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) down in 1994 as the simplest factor with the right classical limit that satisfies the bootstrap. Delius and Gandenberger derived it five years later from the soliton reflection matrix.

**Poles.** In the blocks, $(x)$ has a pole at $\theta=i\pi x/h$, and the physical strip $0<\operatorname{Im}\theta<\frac\pi2$ is $0<x<\frac h2$. The blocks $(h+1-c-\frac B2)$ and $(c-\frac B2)^{-1}$ have no poles there. So for $a\le h/2$ the only physical-strip poles of $K_a$ are simple poles at $\theta=\frac{i\pi p}h$, $p=1,\dots,a-1$, independent of the coupling (checked for $n\le7$ in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`). Delius and Gandenberger explain them by a triangle diagram: particle $a$ decays into $p$ and $a-p$, $p$ reflects off the boundary at rapidity $i\pi a/h$, where $K_p$ has neither a pole nor a zero, and fuses again with $a-p$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, fig. 9]. Three internal lines and one loop give a simple pole (@sec-boundary-coleman-thun). There are no boundary bound states, as in the classical theory, where (-@eq-linear-reflection) at $C=+1$ has no poles in the strip.

**Rank one.** For $n=1$, (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) is $K_1=(2-\frac B2)/\big((1)(1-\frac B2)\big)$. This is the sinh-Gordon factor (-@eq-shg-reflection) at $E=\frac B2$, $F=0$: Ghoshal's factor at $\hat\epsilon=0$, continued. Chenaghlou and Corrigan's conjecture, extended to $C_0=C_1=1$, gives instead $E=0$ (@cnj-shg-e). Since (-@eq-shg-reflection) depends only on $E^2$, the two differ only at $O(B^2)$ (`textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`). So one-loop perturbation theory cannot tell them apart.

The two values belong to two different quantum boundary couplings, both of which are $C\equiv1$ classically. Normalize the action as in perturbed conformal field theory: $\frac1{4\pi}(\partial\phi)^2+2\mu\cosh2b\phi$ in the bulk and $M(e^{b\phi}+e^{-b\phi})$ at the boundary, with $b^2=\beta^2/4\pi=B/(2-B)$. Write $M=M_0\cosh\pi bs$ with $M_0=\sqrt{\mu/\sin\pi b^2}$ [@fzz2000]. Classically $M/M_0\to1$ is $C_0=C_1=1$. The continuation of @cnj-bsg-uv-ir reads $\cos\frac{\pi E}{2-B}=M/M_0$, which is Chenaghlou and Corrigan's relation (@cnj-shg-e) with $C=M/M_0$. It puts $E=\frac B2$ at $M/M_0=\cos\frac{\pi b^2}2=\cos\frac{\pi B}{2(2-B)}$, and $E=0$ at $M=M_0$.

Both assignments have been tested without perturbation theory. The boundary TBA built from (-@eq-shg-reflection) reproduces the ultraviolet behaviour that the boundary Liouville reflection amplitude predicts for the Lagrangian boundary [@brz2008]. With $E=\frac B2$ it does so at $M/M_0=\cos\frac{\pi b^2}2$, to $10^{-14}$, and misses $M=M_0$; with $E=0$ it is the other way round (`textbook_code/shg_boundary_tba.py`).

Which of the two couplings is the uniform boundary is decided by $n\ge2$. There classical integrability leaves no free boundary parameter ($|C_j|=1$), and the quantum boundary coupling is taken to be $\mu_B^2=\frac\mu2\cot\frac{\pi b^2}2$, which tends to the classical $\mu_B^2=\mu/\pi b^2$ as $b\to0$. This value is not derived from integrability. Fateev obtained it as the condition for the boundary of the conformal Toda theory to preserve $W$-symmetry. He, and Ahn, Kim and Rim, assume that the integrable affine boundary is this conformal boundary perturbed by the affine terms [@fateev2001; @akr2002]. The assumption has numerical support: with (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) as input, the boundary TBA reproduces the ultraviolet data at this coupling for $a_2^{(1)}$, $a_3^{(1)}$ and $a_4^{(1)}$ [@akr2002]. At $n=1$ the same formula is $M/M_0=\cos\frac{\pi b^2}2$. Fateev's conjectured ground-state energy of this boundary [@fateev2001] equals the sinh-Gordon boundary energy at $E=\frac B2$, and differs from the one at $E=0$ by $-\frac{\pi m}{16}\frac B2+O(B^2)$ (`textbook_code/shg_boundary_tba.py`).

On this evidence the quantum uniform boundary carries the renormalized coupling $M/M_0=\cos\frac{\pi b^2}2$ for every $n$. For $n=1$ this is the point $\hat\epsilon=0$, with $E=\frac B2$, as (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) says. The coupling $M=M_0$, with $E=0$, is a different member of the sinh-Gordon family that classically has the same $C_0=C_1=1$. For sine-Gordon, Zamolodchikov's relation puts $\hat\epsilon=0$ at $\tilde\mu/\tilde\mu_{\rm crit}=\cos\frac\pi{2(\lambda+1)}$ (@sec-bsg-parameters), the continuation of the same point.

## The Neumann boundary and duality {#sec-neumann-duality}

The bulk S-matrices are invariant under $B\to2-B$, the weak–strong duality $\beta\to4\pi/\beta$ (@sec-strong-weak). Every block $\{x\}$ is invariant separately, so the bulk S-matrices are self-dual. The reflection amplitudes (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) are not: the blocks $(h+1-c-\frac B2)$ and $(c-\frac B2)$ are not invariant. Corrigan observed that the sinh-Gordon reflection factors obtained from Ghoshal's breather factors are in general not self-dual, and that duality relates different boundary conditions rather than mapping each to itself [@corrigan1998]. Gandenberger found for $a_2^{(1)}$ that the dual of the uniform amplitude is the Neumann amplitude [@gandenberger1999a]. Delius and Gandenberger conjectured the same for all $n$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (3.20)]:

$$
K^N_a(\theta)=K_a(\theta)\big|_{B\to2-B}=\prod_{c=1}^a\frac{(c-1)\,\big(h-c+\frac B2\big)}{(h-c)\,\big(c-1+\frac B2\big)} .
$$ {#eq-neumann-amplitude}

::: {#cnj-neumann-amplitude}
## Particle reflection off the Neumann boundary
**[Conjecture]** The reflection amplitudes of the particles of real-coupling $a_n^{(1)}$ theory off the Neumann boundary $C_j\equiv0$ are (-@eq-neumann-amplitude).
:::

What is checked (`textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`):

- (-@eq-neumann-amplitude) satisfies unitarity, crossing-unitarity, the bulk boundary bootstrap at every fusing, and $K^N_a=K^N_{h-a}$, for $n\le7$. This is automatic, since every axiom is invariant under $B\to2-B$.
- As $B\to0$, $K^N_a\to1$, the linearized Neumann factor (@sec-classical-reflection-factors).
- **One loop.** With $B=\frac{\beta^2}{2\pi}+O(\beta^4)$ and $(x+\frac B2)/(x)=1+\frac{i\pi B}{2h}\frac{\sinh\theta}{\cosh\theta-\cos(\pi x/h)}+O(B^2)$, the $O(\beta^2)$ terms of $K^N_1$ and $K^N_2$ for $a_3^{(1)}$ are exactly Kim's one-loop Neumann amplitudes [@kim1995, eqs. (33), (39)]; the uniform amplitude does not reproduce them. For $a_2^{(1)}$ the $O(\beta^2)$ term of $K^N_1$ is $-\frac14\frac{\cos(\theta/2i)}{\sin(3\theta/2i)}\beta^2$, as given by Gandenberger, who reports agreement with Kim [@gandenberger1999a, eq. (6.11)].
- For $n=1$, (-@eq-neumann-amplitude) is (-@eq-shg-reflection) at $E=1-\frac B2$, $F=0$, Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's Neumann point.

Kim had proposed exact Neumann amplitudes by assuming self-duality [@kim1995]. They agree with (-@eq-neumann-amplitude) at one loop, which is all his calculation could test, but not beyond (checked for $n=2,\dots,6$ in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`). The same applies to the other self-dual proposals of the period [@fring_koberle1994a; @sasaki1993], as Delius and Gandenberger point out.

**Which soliton reflection matrix?** Delius and Gandenberger obtained the uniform amplitude from the diagonal soliton reflection matrix, and the Neumann amplitude only as its dual. The soliton route to the Neumann amplitude needs the soliton reflection matrix of the Neumann boundary. Following Delius and MacKay [@delius_mackay2003], one would take this to be the diagonal one. It is not: by @cnj-neumann-coideal, the Neumann boundary has coideal parameters $\hat\epsilon_j=\epsilon_*$ and the non-diagonal reflection matrix (-@eq-an-k-matrix) with $s=+1$, and the diagonal matrix belongs to $C\equiv+1$ (@sec-epsilon-constraint).

With the scalar factor (-@eq-an-nondiagonal-scalar), the $s=+1$ matrix gives the Neumann amplitude directly. Its lowest-breather amplitude is (-@eq-an-neumann-breather), and $\omega\to-2/B$ turns it into
$$
\Big(-\frac n2\omega\Big)_I\Big(\frac n2\omega-\frac12\Big)_I\Big(\frac12\Big)_I\ \longrightarrow\ (-n)\Big(n+\frac B2\Big)\Big(-\frac B2\Big)=K^N_1 ,
$$
the first amplitude of (-@eq-neumann-amplitude); the heavier particles follow by the bulk bootstrap, as for the uniform boundary. For $n=2$ this is Gandenberger's $K^{(+)}_1=(-2)(-\frac B2)(2+\frac B2)$ [@gandenberger1999a, eq. (6.4)]. The scalar factor reproduces the leading semiclassical Neumann time advance (@sec-boundary-semiclassics). For $n=3$ Kim's one-loop amplitudes require a CDD factor, and the factor $P_{\omega/2}=(\frac T2-\frac\omega2)_I(\frac T2+\frac\omega2)_I$ in (-@eq-an-nondiagonal-scalar) reproduces them, but one loop does not fix it uniquely (@sec-an-nondiagonal-k). So, given @cnj-neumann-coideal and @cnj-reflection-continuation, (-@eq-neumann-amplitude) is now derived from the soliton side, numerically for $n=2,3,4$ (`textbook_code/an_nondiagonal_scalar.py`), with one proviso: the CDD factor is chosen to give exact duality with the uniform amplitude.

**The third matrix.** The $s=-1$ matrix, with its scalar factor (-@eq-an-nondiagonal-scalar-minus), reflects the lowest breather with the amplitude (-@eq-an-minus-breather). Under $\omega\to-2/B$ it becomes
$$
-\Big(\frac\omega2\Big)_I\Big(\frac12-T\Big)_I\Big(-\frac\omega2-\frac12\Big)_I\ \longrightarrow\ K^{(-)}_1=-(1)\Big(h-\frac B2\Big)\Big(-1+\frac B2\Big)=-(1)(h-1)\,K_1 ,
$$
with $K_1$ the uniform amplitude (-@eq-uniform-amplitude), and the bootstrap gives $K^{(-)}_a=-(a)(h-a)\,K_a$. For $a_2^{(1)}$ this is Gandenberger's $K^{(-)}_1=-(1)(-1+\frac B2)(3-\frac B2)$ [@gandenberger1999a, eq. (6.4)]. For $n\le7$ these amplitudes satisfy all the axioms and tend to 1 as $B\to0$, like the Neumann amplitude. Their duals $-(a)(h-a)\,K^N_a$ are the amplitudes that Corrigan et al. conjectured for $C\equiv-1$ [@cdrs1994, eq. (5.16)], for every $a$; for $n=2$ this is their "minimal" amplitude $-(1)(2+\frac B2)/(\frac B2)$ [@cdrs1994, eq. (5.7)] (`textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`). The derivation from the soliton side is numerical for $n\le4$ (@prp-an-nondiagonal-scalar), and like the Neumann one it assumes @cnj-reflection-continuation. No boundary condition is known for $s=-1$. The coideal analysis thus gives a third quantum boundary, with $\hat\epsilon_0=-\epsilon_*$ and $\hat\epsilon_{j\ge1}=\epsilon_*$, that the classical classification of @sec-durham-classification does not contain.

**Duality on the half-line.** Duality is therefore not a symmetry of any single half-line theory we know. It exchanges the boundary conditions $C\equiv+1$ and $C\equiv0$, as for sinh-Gordon [@corrigan1998; @corrigan_delius1999]. On the soliton side the two have different kinds of reflection matrix ($\hat\epsilon=0$ and $\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_*$), so the duality cannot come from a symmetry of the coideals at fixed $\omega$. It relates the theory at $\beta$ to the one at $4\pi/\beta$, that is, $\omega$ to $\omega'=-\omega/(\omega+1)$, and how the coideal parameters transform under it is not known.

## Solitonic boundary conditions {#sec-solitonic-boundaries}

For a sign pattern $C_j\in\{\pm1\}$ with $\prod_jC_j=1$, not all $+1$, the vacuum is a stationary soliton held in front of the boundary and continued to real coupling (@prp-solitonic-vacua). Its topological charge $\vec\lambda$ is fixed by $(-1)^{\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\lambda}=C_j$ and is a weight of a fundamental representation $\Lambda_b$, with $b$ given by @prp-dg-weights. The energy of the vacuum is (-@eq-vacuum-energy). At imaginary coupling the picture is a stationary soliton, carrying the charge $\vec\lambda$, sitting in front of a boundary which, relative to the vacuum between them, is the uniform boundary $C\equiv+1$ (@sec-images-boundary).

**The amplitude.** By factorization, a breather reflecting off this configuration passes the stationary soliton, reflects off the uniform boundary and passes the soliton again [@delius_gandenberger1999, fig. 8]. The breather–soliton S-matrix does not depend on which member of the multiplet the soliton is [@gandenberger1998], so the result is diagonal. Delius and Gandenberger computed the product of the two scatterings at imaginary coupling [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (5.3)] and continued it. In book blocks, the particle amplitudes are

$$
K^{(b)}_a(\theta)=K_a(\theta)\,M^{(b)}_a(\theta),\qquad
M^{(b)}_a=\prod_{k=1}^a\frac{\big(a+b+\frac h2-2k+\frac B2\big)\big(b-a-\frac h2+2k-\frac B2\big)}{\big(a+b-\frac h2-2k+\frac B2\big)\big(b-a+\frac h2+2k-\frac B2\big)} ,
$$ {#eq-solitonic-factor}

with $K_a$ the uniform amplitude (-@eq-uniform-amplitude) [@delius_gandenberger1999, eqs. (5.4), (5.5)]. For odd $h$ the blocks sit at half-integer positions.

::: {#prp-solitonic-amplitude}
## Properties of the solitonic amplitudes
**[Numerical]** For $n=2,\dots,6$ and all $a,b$:

(i) $K^{(b)}_a$ satisfies boundary unitarity, crossing-unitarity in both forms, $K^{(b)}_a=K^{(b)}_{h-a}$, and the bulk boundary bootstrap at every fusing;
(ii) $M^{(b)}_a=M^{(h-b)}_a$;
(iii) as $B\to0$, $M^{(b)}_a\to\big(a+b-\frac h2\big)\big(-a-b-\frac h2\big)\big(a-b+\frac h2\big)\big(b-a+\frac h2\big)$, DG (5.7);
(iv) the $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_4^{(1)}$ vacuum amplitudes DG (6.3), (6.18), (6.19), (6.25) are special cases, and so is (6.26) once a missing block is restored (@sec-particle-reflection-notes).
:::

Checked in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`. That these are the amplitudes of the solitonic boundaries assumes @cnj-reflection-continuation. Item (ii) is needed for consistency, since $\vec\lambda$ and $-\vec\lambda$, which lie in $\Lambda_b$ and $\Lambda_{h-b}$, give the same vacuum. It also has a striking consequence. **All solitonic boundary conditions whose weight lies in $\Lambda_b$ or $\Lambda_{h-b}$ have the same particle reflection amplitudes**, although their classical vacua look different. The $2^n-1$ solitonic patterns fall into $\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$ quantum equivalence classes, one for each pair $\{b,h-b\}$. For $a_2^{(1)}$ there is one class, $(+--)$, $(-+-)$, $(--+)$. For $a_4^{(1)}$ there are two: five patterns with $b\in\{1,4\}$ and ten with $b\in\{2,3\}$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 6.4]. The classical limit (iii) is Bowcock's linearized reflection factor about the continued vacuum [@bowcock1998, (4.14), (4.21), (4.22)].

**What is assumed.** Besides @cnj-reflection-continuation:

- *The vacuum.* That the continued soliton has the lowest energy (assumption 2). For the alternating patterns of $a_3^{(1)}$ and the other missing patterns of @tbl-missing-vacua no regular classical vacuum is known; only boundary-singular configurations that are energy infima (@sec-boundary-missing-charges). Delius and Gandenberger's formula assigns them the amplitude of their class anyway. This is a prediction, and it supports Delius's suggestion that the missing vacua exist (@sec-boundary-missing-charges).
- *The modulus.* The classical vacuum has a modulus $\chi$ (@prp-solitonic-vacua), and the formula does not depend on it. Delius and Gandenberger argue that the quantum theory has a unique ground state. The spectrum of @sec-boundary-spectrum-a2 suggests where the modulus goes: the tower $b_{n,-n}$, whose energies tend to zero as $B\to0$.
- *$C\equiv-1$ for even $h$.* This pattern is solitonic of type $b=h/2$, with the self-conjugate vacuum family of @prp-self-conjugate-vacuum, and also has the vacuum $\vec\phi=0$ at the same energy. Corrigan et al.'s conjecture for $C\equiv-1$ [@cdrs1994] is built on $\vec\phi=0$ and differs from (-@eq-solitonic-factor). Delius and Gandenberger read this as two vacuum sectors [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 7].

**Poles.** Unlike $K_a$, the factor $M^{(b)}_a$ has coupling-dependent poles in the physical strip. For $a_2^{(1)}$, $b=1$: $M^{(1)}_1=(\frac12-\frac B2)(\frac32-\frac B2)(\frac32+\frac B2)(\frac52+\frac B2)$, with poles at $\theta=\frac{i\pi}3(\frac12-\frac B2)$ (for $B<1$) and $\theta=\frac{i\pi}3(\frac32-\frac B2)$. These are boundary bound states, and they start the spectrum of the next section. For $a_3^{(1)}$, $b=2$, the vacuum amplitude $K_1^{(2)}=K_1\,(1-\frac B2)^2(3+\frac B2)^2$ even has a double pole at $\theta=\frac{i\pi}4(1-\frac B2)$.

## The boundary spectrum of a_2 {#sec-boundary-spectrum-a2}

Take $a_2^{(1)}$ with a solitonic boundary ($h=3$) and $0<B<1$. The vacuum amplitude $K^{b_{0,0}}_1=K^{b_{0,0}}_2$ is DG (6.3), the case $a=b=1$ of (-@eq-solitonic-factor). Its two physical-strip poles are boundary bound states, and the boundary bootstrap (-@eq-boundary-bootstrap) gives the amplitudes off the excited states, whose poles give further states, and so on. **One step in detail.** By (-@eq-solitonic-factor) the vacuum amplitude is $K^{b_{0,0}}_1=K_1\,(\frac12-\frac B2)(\frac32-\frac B2)(\frac32+\frac B2)(\frac52+\frac B2)$. The block $(\frac12-\frac B2)$ has its pole at $\theta=iv$, $v=\frac\pi6(1-B)$, inside the physical strip for $0<B<1$. As a bound state of particle 1 it raises the boundary energy by $m_1\cos v$ (-@eq-boundary-bound-state-energy), which is $0.9588\,m_1$ at $B=\frac9{20}$. The boundary bootstrap (-@eq-boundary-bootstrap) gives the amplitude of particle 1 on the new state as $K^{b_{0,0}}_1(\theta)\,S_{11}(\theta-iv)\,S_{11}(\theta+iv)$, with $S_{11}=\{1\}=(0)(2)/\big((B)(2-B)\big)$ by (-@eq-an-smatrix). The shift identity $(x)(\theta+\frac{i\pi p}h)\,(x)(\theta-\frac{i\pi p}h)=(x+p)(x-p)$ of @exr-ly-excited, with $p=\frac12-\frac B2$, turns the two S-matrices into
$$
\frac{(\frac52-\frac B2)(\frac32+\frac B2)}{(\frac12+\frac B2)(-\frac12+\frac{3B}2)(\frac52-\frac{3B}2)(\frac32-\frac B2)} .
$$
The factor $(\frac32-\frac B2)^{-1}$ removes the second pole of the vacuum amplitude, and the product is the amplitude of the state $b_{1,0}$ below (checked numerically in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`). Its pole at $\frac12-\frac B2$ survives; on $b_{1,0}$ it is the crossed process, with $b_{0,0}$ in the intermediate state, as explained after (-@eq-a2-excited). Repeating the step gives all the states.

Delius and Gandenberger label the states $b_{n,m}$, where $n$ and $m$ count bound particles of type 1 and 2, and found [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (6.7)]

$$
\begin{aligned}
K^{b_{n,m}}_1(\theta)=K_1(\theta)\;&\Big(\tfrac12-(2n+1)\tfrac B2\Big)\Big(\tfrac52+(2m+1)\tfrac B2\Big)\;\Big(\tfrac12-(2n-1)\tfrac B2\Big)\Big(\tfrac52+(2m-1)\tfrac B2\Big)\\
\times\;&\Big(\tfrac32+(2n-1)\tfrac B2\Big)\Big(\tfrac32-(2m-1)\tfrac B2\Big)\;\Big(-\tfrac52+(2n+1)\tfrac B2\Big)\Big(-\tfrac12-(2m+1)\tfrac B2\Big),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-a2-excited}

with $K_1$ of (-@eq-breather-continuation) and $K^{b_{n,m}}_2=K^{b_{m,n}}_1$. The display contains four pairs of blocks, which we call its four lines, as in DG (6.7). Each pair has the form $\big(x(n,m)\big)\big(h-x(m,n)\big)$, which makes crossing-unitarity manifest.

::: {#prp-a2-excited}
## The excited-state amplitudes of $a_2^{(1)}$
**[Numerical]** For $-3\le n,m\le3$: (i) (-@eq-a2-excited) satisfies boundary unitarity, crossing-unitarity (with $K^{b_{n,m}}_2=K^{b_{m,n}}_1$) and the bulk bootstrap $K_2=K_1(\theta+\frac{i\pi}3)S_{11}(2\theta)K_1(\theta-\frac{i\pi}3)$ on every state; (ii) the boundary bootstrap (-@eq-boundary-bootstrap) holds for particle 1 bound at $\theta=\frac{i\pi}3\big(\frac12-(2n+1)\frac B2\big)$, taking $b_{n,m}$ to $b_{n+1,m}$; for particle 2 bound at $\frac{i\pi}3\big(\frac12-(2m+1)\frac B2\big)$, taking $b_{n,m}$ to $b_{n,m+1}$; and for particle 1 bound to $b_{-n,n}$ at $\frac{i\pi}3\big(\frac32-(2n+1)\frac B2\big)$, taking it to $b_{-n-1,n+1}$; (iii) DG (6.3), (6.6), (6.9) and (6.10) are special cases. (`textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`)
:::

That these are the amplitudes off the excited states of the solitonic boundary assumes @cnj-reflection-continuation, as for the vacuum amplitude.

**Energies.** By (-@eq-boundary-bound-state-energy), each step adds $m_1\cos v$, with $iv$ the pole at which the particle binds. Summing along the steps of @prp-a2-excited gives a closed form (checked along all three kinds of step in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`):

$$
e_{b_{n,m}}-e_{b_{0,0}}=m_1\big[F(n)+F(m)\big],\qquad F(k)=\frac{\sin k\delta\,\cos(\frac\pi6-k\delta)}{\sin\delta},\qquad\delta=\frac{\pi B}6 ,
$$ {#eq-a2-energies}

valid for negative $k$ too, with $m_1$ the renormalized particle mass. In particular $e_{b_{n,-n}}-e_{b_{0,0}}=m_1\sin^2(n\delta)/\sin\delta$.

**Which poles are states.** Not every pole of (-@eq-a2-excited) is a new state. Delius and Gandenberger account for them, for $n+m>0$, as follows [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 6.2, figs. 10–12]:

- the first block of the first line creates $b_{n+1,m}$;
- the first block of the second line is the crossed process, with $b_{n-1,m}$ in the intermediate state;
- the second block of the third line (for $m>0$), and its first block (for $n\le0$), come from boundary Coleman–Thun diagrams in which the reflection in the middle happens at a zero of the reflection factor, so the naive double pole becomes simple (@sec-boundary-coleman-thun).

For $n+m=0$ the second and fourth lines cancel, and the pole of $(\frac32-(2n+1)\frac B2)$ creates $b_{-n-1,n+1}$. When two Coleman–Thun diagrams contribute at the same point, as for $b_{0,1}$, where the two blocks of the third line coincide, the pole is double. On $b_{n,-n}$ with $B>2/(2n-1)$ a further pole, at $p=\frac52-(2n-1)\frac B2$, comes from a third diagram [@delius_gandenberger1999, fig. 12c]; at $B=\frac9{20}$ this is the pole of $K_1$ on $b_{3,-3}$ in @tbl-a2-boundary-states. The poles that create states leave the physical strip as $n$ or $m$ grows, so the spectrum is finite [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 6.2]:

$$
b_{n,m}\ \text{with}\ n+m>0,\ |n|,|m|<\tfrac1{2B}+\tfrac12;\qquad b_{n,-n},\,b_{-n,n}\ \text{with}\ 0\le n<\tfrac3{2B}+\tfrac12 .
$$

This range seems to leave one pole unexplained. On $b_{-n,n}$ the pole $p=\frac12+(2n-1)\frac B2$, which Delius and Gandenberger attribute to the creation of $b_{-n+1,n}$, is in the physical strip for $B<\frac2{2n-1}$, while $b_{-n+1,n}$ lies in the range only for $B<\frac1{2n-1}$. At $B=\frac9{20}$ this is the pole $\frac{47}{40}$ on $b_{-2,2}$ in @tbl-a2-boundary-states (and on $b_{2,-2}$ for $K_2$).

In the window $\frac1{2n-1}<B<\frac2{2n-1}$ this pole is not a bound state but a boundary Coleman–Thun pole. Three facts show it.

- **The sign of the residue.** A bound-state pole has $-i\operatorname{Res}K=\frac12g^2>0$ at real coupling (@sec-boundary-bound-states). Here $-i\operatorname{Res}K_1$ is positive below the window, changes sign at $B=\frac1{2n-1}$, where the pole meets the pole at $\frac32-(2n-1)\frac B2$, and is negative inside it. At $B=\frac9{20}$ it is $-1.187$.
- **A threshold.** At $B=\frac1{2n-1}$ the state $b_{-n+1,n}$ reaches the threshold of $b_{-n+1,n-1}$ plus a particle 2 at rest. Its creation pole in $K_2^{b_{-n+1,n-1}}$, at $p=\frac12-(2n-1)\frac B2$, passes through $\theta=0$ with vanishing residue. Above the threshold the strip contains instead a zero, at $\theta_R=\frac{i\pi}3\big((2n-1)\frac B2-\frac12\big)$, and $b_{-n+1,n}$ is a virtual state.
- **A diagram.** Exactly in the window there is a boundary Coleman–Thun diagram. $b_{-n,n}$ emits a particle 1 and drops to $b_{-n+1,n-1}$. The incoming particle 1 fuses with the emitted one into a particle 2, which reflects at $\theta_R$, at the zero, and splits back, and the emitted particle is reabsorbed. The diagram has two loops and would give a double pole; the zero makes it simple.

The residue has the form of this diagram. Combining the boundary and bulk bootstraps gives exactly $\operatorname{Res}K_1^{b_{-n,n}}=\frac12g^2\Gamma^2\,K_2^{b_{-n+1,n-1}}{}'(\theta_R)$, where $\frac i2g^2$ is the residue that creates $b_{-n,n}$ from $b_{-n+1,n-1}$ and $i\Gamma^2$ that of $S_{11}$ at $\frac{2\pi i}3$. The signs and this identity are checked for $n=2,3,4$ in `textbook_code/particle_reflection.py`. The spectrum of Delius and Gandenberger therefore stands.

The lower bound $n+m\ge0$ is imposed so that no state lies below the ground state $b_{0,0}$; for instance $e_{b_{-1,0}}-e_{b_{0,0}}=-m_1\cos(\frac\pi6+\delta)<0$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 6.2].

| state | reached from | by particle, at $\theta=\frac{i\pi p}3$ | $p$ | $(e-e_{b_{0,0}})/m_1$ | poles of $K_1$ in the strip ($p$) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $b_{0,0}$ | ground state | — | — | 0 | $\frac{11}{40}$, $\frac{51}{40}$ |
| $b_{-1,1}$ | $b_{0,0}$ | 1 | $\frac32-\frac B2=\frac{51}{40}$ | 0.2334 | $\frac{29}{40}$, $\frac{33}{40}$, $\frac{51}{40}$ |
| $b_{1,-1}$ | $b_{0,0}$ | 2 | $\frac{51}{40}$ | 0.2334 | none |
| $b_{-2,2}$ | $b_{-1,1}$ | 1 | $\frac32-\frac{3B}2=\frac{33}{40}$ | 0.8829 | $\frac{3}{8}$, $\frac{33}{40}$, $\frac{47}{40}$ |
| $b_{2,-2}$ | $b_{1,-1}$ | 2 | $\frac{33}{40}$ | 0.8829 | none |
| $b_{1,0}$ | $b_{0,0}$ | 1 | $\frac12-\frac B2=\frac{11}{40}$ | 0.9588 | $\frac{11}{40}$ |
| $b_{0,1}$ | $b_{0,0}$ | 2 | $\frac{11}{40}$ | 0.9588 | $\frac{11}{40}$, $\frac{29}{40}$, $\frac{51}{40}$ (double) |
